utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue, I'd first like to deal with the documents tendered through the last witness, but I'm not quite sure whether the videotapes are ready thus that we know exactly how they are tendered and how they will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar suggests to me and I think it's a very wise suggestion that we wait until all the copies and the compilations are available in the way in which the parties intend to tender them and then deal with all the documents and videotapes at the same time. Meanwhile, I inform the parties that the first BBC tape, so to say, has been copied and is available for the parties. The second BBC tape is on its way to be copied and we expect them to be delivered to the parties today. That also means that if there would be any -- if the parties would insist on accepting the -- what was offered by the witness yesterday, that is to review the tapes, that a start could be made but only in respect of the BBC one tape because that's the only one available at this very moment. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Very respectfully, the Defence doesn't quite see the problem in relation to the copies of the videotapes because what Defence wishes to produce is the compilated extract of what they have already submitted, 8 or 9 extracts that we have already submitted in the examination-in-chief and I think on the other side what could be tendered are just excerpts that were viewed in the cross-examination so I think at the level of the evidence, I do not see what the problem is well evident because there are many, many more extracts compared to the ones that were viewed here in the Chamber -- before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that you had 9, I think it was 9 sequences played. They are on a separate tape, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They're on one videotape. We put it all on one tape which is in the hands of the registrar, so as far as we are concerned, Mr. President, we would tender that reconstituted tape and the copy, I believe, was handed over to the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Prosecution is not tendering any video apart from -- no additional videos will be tendered, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President. We've so far tendered two compilation tapes. One of those compilation tapes has on it only one segment, what one might call the French convoy. The other has, I think 7 or 9 excerpts. We may, for convenience sake, copy the -- what we might call the brown Mercedes excerpt on to a separate tape as well. That is in evidence that has been shown to the witness and as I indicated yesterday, we have a transcript now for that as well. Beyond that, president, the issues are whether somewhere on the tapes there is an image of the crater which, according to the witness, was involved with the market explosion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that is a separate issue it's a matter of whether the Prosecution seeks to tender that at a later stage if it exists on that tape or not. So there would be no need to wait on a decision of the admission into evidence of the tapes that are available now. Is the part played by you, is that the -- the quality, is that there's no problem with the quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is the other issue, Mr. President., in particular in relation to the shelling of the parliamentary offices. The excerpt which the Prosecution has so far tendered has a lot of distortion on it which is not on the original tape and I would seek to replace that segment with a cleaner copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then if the parties would please it's clear already for the Defence but I'd like to have a very short brief note that says this version of this videotape is tendered and let's then deal with it in the next few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, but we will have a problem because bearing in mind our position, we handed over the tape with 9 excerpts. Each one of these excerpts has been viewed in the courtroom. On the other side, now the Prosecution says that they will deliver a sort of best of with all 9 or 10 excerpts but we have not viewed them before the Chamber. We have seen some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... That's exactly the reason why I suggest that we'll wait until we know for certain what it exactly is and what version, what quality, and then deal with the matter as a whole. I think that a delayed decision on that would not harm the interest of either party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next issue we still have to deal with is the time available for the parties to examine their experts. The Chamber has compared the number of witnesses, the subject matter of expert witnesses and we have given a decision already in respect of some expert witnesses and how much time would be available. I'm, for example, referring to the background witnesses of which the last one still has to be examined that's Mr. Terzic. On those witnesses that are still to be examined, and where the parties have explained to the Chamber how much time they will need, the Chamber has considered how much time will be granted. In respect of the expert witness, Mr. Kuljic, the Chamber considers that 45 minutes for the Defence and two hours for the Prosecution would be fair. In respect of the expert witness Vilicic, who is the first one to be examined as far as I understand, the Chamber has considered how much time would be needed and in a very strict regime, has decided to give five and a half hours to both parties. In respect to the expert witness Radinovic, the -- it might be a matter of language but both parties, five and a half hours. Then in respect of Radinovic, the Chamber has granted three hours, the Defence has asked for more. The Chamber has decided that both Defence and Prosecution will be granted four hours in respect of Radinovic. The Chamber is aware that viewing the list of documents the Defence seeks to tender through that witness and -- seems to be a lot of new documents that might cause some problems, at the same time and under normal circumstances, the Chamber considers it the normal course of events that the documents on which an expert relies, that they are included in the footnote material, for example, and that is presented as an annex to or footnotes in the report. The Chamber is, of course, not aware what these documents exactly are all about, but the Chamber suggests to the Defence that a system of glossary would be added to that and the expert witness would be invited just to write a few words for each document indicating for what reason this expert thinks that is an important or a relevant document. That could also be done for a group of documents. If, for example, we would see 10 combat reports or 30 combat reports of, let's say, March 1993, and if the expert will think that these are relevant documents because it illustrates the fierce fighting during that month in the front, well, let's say in the Stup area, then just a short comment could be added to those 30 documents saying: "Illustration of fierce fighting in Stup in the month of March 1993 or 1994." That could also facilitate the introduction of these documents. The Chamber of course has not taken any decision on whether it will admit these documents or not but the Chamber is aware that if, during four hours, you want to introduce 100 documents, that that would be two and a half minutes for each document and therefore this is a suggestion to the Defence how to deal with it in such a way that there is still a chance of these documents to be admitted without using all its time on just presenting documents. The Chamber also thinks that the Defence should inform the Prosecution as to what documents will be tendered into evidence so that there's no uncertainty that the Prosecution can prepare for cross-examination, that they can know what they can expect in respect of these documents. That was about the expert witness Radinovic. We -- I think on Terzic, we have -- I first go through the list and then give you an opportunity, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, to make observations. In respect of Terzic, I think there's ten minutes for the Defence left. The Chamber deems one hour for the Prosecution sufficient time to cross-examine Mr. Terzic. In respect of Radovanovic, two hours for the Defence, two hours for the Prosecution should be sufficient. The Chamber emphasises that whenever an expert witness appears, that the Chamber has thoroughly read the report and that there is no need to make the expert witness repeat what is already in his or her report. If there are any observations in respect of this decision, please make them. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, first of all, thank you and as far as the expert Radinovic is concerned, we have time to confer in this respect. We will ask the expert to make a kind of vulgate and if he can proceed to make as brief a summary as possible, a kind of vulgarisation as we've already explained now, what the Defence does not wish to happen is that this summary becomes a subject of dispute between the parties, that is when things are being summarised, necessarily things become condensed and then positions become entrenched and we do not wish that this starts off discussions whatsoever. That was the first point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Clarify the position of the Chamber. I think it's not that much a summary not even a brief summary but within the Chamber, the words -- I don't know how to pronounce it in English but in the ancient, in the history of law on the European continent, I think it was Roman law, glossatori that means brief remarks attached to a text. So not a summary but just a brief comment. It could be three, four, five words, might be and that's what the Chamber has in mind, not to a summary but rather a reference to relevance or -- well, what is the use of looking at this document in view of the case of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But Mr. President, we will then ask the expert Radinovic to be his own glossatori or glossary maker so we will do this. Another point was the point of time. We took note of your decision and we will have to discuss it with General Galic who was trying to say something to his counsel earlier and the third important point was that of the exhibits. Your decision places us in a slightly delicate decision because it frequently appears that things are clear but only it is in the course of the session and we don't think that it is necessary to tender such and such an exhibit, we don't think that's necessary to tender such an exhibit to add to the pile. So I'm not in a position to say that I will tender everything to make sure that everything is there, I think you have to understand that our position could change, that is, evolve and develop. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... As far as documents are concerned, let's keep in mind that we are talking about expert witnesses and where the case law is that facts on which they base themselves should be established should not be contested anymore. So an expert witness is not a vehicle to establish a lot of facts but to hear the expert opinion on facts established or sometimes on facts clearly assumed in order to follow the reasoning of the expert. Yes, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please, Mr. President, Your Honours, may I respectfully add that, of course, we accept and adopt the decision in respect of the time and we observe, I would like to observe nonetheless that I would respectfully apply for liberty to review the time afforded the Prosecution depending upon what happens. Mr. President, you have indicated that the report has already been thoroughly read by the Court, therefore five and a half hours for the Defence logically would be something in addition to it and in furtherance of the report and it might leave the Prosecution in difficulty to have the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- the Chamber does understand that and as you might have noticed, that during the Prosecution's case, sometimes the party introducing a certain report took more time than the cross-examining party. This is, for example, what happened for the expert Phillips. The Chamber has also taken into consideration the type of information contained in the report, so it's not without reason that for Terzic there's only ten minutes for the Defence left and one hour for the Prosecution. We have seen, during the presentation of the Prosecution's case, that it very much depends on the subject matter on how to divide time among the parties; therefore, for Vilicic, it's for quite sometime, it's for both parties but I add to that that we want to hear expert opinion rather than repeat a repetition of the report and establishing of facts and in respect of Vilicic, also taking into consideration how much time there was used during the examination of Zecevic, Kovacs and Higgs which are, more or less, the counterparts, I would say, of Vilicic, there the parties took approximately the same time for examination-in-chief and cross-examination. There was also then the Chamber had thoroughly read the report so this is I explained just a few more reasons as you may see the Chamber has thoroughly considered a lot of aspects before granting time to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As it please, Mr. President, I'm sure the court will apply its discretion appropriately, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, merely to sum up and I only want to know this with regard to Witness Vilicic, we have decided to ask him to repeat certain things but to put them in lay language because he has given us mathematical formulae and they are the difficult to grasp and therefore we shall ask him to explain certain things so that we shall be doing it only to have him repeat some of these things in a language otherwise there will be no repetition, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I expect, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if, for example, you would look at page 23 of the English version of the report, "the final solution of the above integral can be formulated as equation B," I think it's of no use to present every single detail of this formula to the Chamber. On most parts, the expert has explained clearly which elements are contained in a formula, which elements have been taken into consideration. Don't expect the Chamber to first follow a course in mathematics or in whatever and then being able to analyse each and every part of the formula but the general meaning of the formula, of course, has been explained in the report, tables are quite clear as angles and distances and swathes and the Chamber has carefully considered that. If there would be any specific question on the content of a formula for example Y on the lowest line you say it's a cosine instead of sine, then I would expect that the expert from the Prosecution would whisper that question into the ear of the cross-examining party and if, finally, there would be disagreement which I would say would be disagreement between the experts than disagreement between the parties because I take it that with your education in law you might not be able to follow every single detail of the formula, then of course the Chamber will have to consider that and see its way through such disagreements. Therefore, limit the repetition. The Chamber was fully aware to know the distance between the velocity at firing and the drop velocity and all these kinds of things we really spent a lot of time in preparing the same trajectories, pictures are quite clear, there's no need to repeat all that. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. I rise briefly to make a few comments with respect to the expert, General Radinovic. The Prosecution well comes the Trial Chamber's suggestions to the Defence with respect to a glossary but again our position is and has been consistently that we will need perhaps a significant period of time to explore with this witness both his report as well as the underlying sources thereunder. We also have expressed some concern with respect to the large number of potential exhibits and I understand that that is covered under the proposal which the Chamber just put forth but we also would like to stress, as Your Honour did just a few moments ago, that the law presumes that expert reports are based upon established facts and if the Defence is at this point coming in with approximately 130 proposed exhibits to be tendered through this expert, the Prosecution simply would like to preserve its right to seek additional time both with respect to cross-examining the witness on that large number of exhibits, but also to explore with him in length, if necessary, the extent to which those additional exhibits may or may not have been incorporated into his report. Again, we have consistently taken the view that this statement of this witness is not necessarily supported by or does not necessarily refer to the source material which he indicates he relied upon. And in the event that he then relies upon an additional large number of exhibits, that may require us to seek leave to extend the period of time to cross-examine him on those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that, but the Chamber has already expressed in view of these documents that the Chamber does not know what the content is. The Chamber has not seen the glossary. That means that if 50 documents, you would say this is just a demonstrate that there was ongoing combat during two or three months, then of course we would first see whether that is in dispute, there might be no dispute at all about it so the Chamber is also walking in a -- in the dark more or less in this respect. We have given a decision how much time need and of course especially on an expert witness, for who it's still unclear what is the basis for his expert opinion, we'll have to consider what happens during the examination, but that is, I would say, more the case as far as this expert witness is concerned as in respect to other expert witnesses where we have not a similar problem of so many documents still to be tendered or introduced or tendered from the bar table -- we are not sure on how the Defence intends to do that. At the same time, the Chamber was concerned about a huge number and the time available for the Defence and therefore suggested how to smooth the introduction, emphasising at the same time that this does not say anything about whether we will admit or not admit the documents in evidence and finally I'd make one observation that is that as from several decisions of this Chamber may have become clear that the -- I would say the classical distinction between the weighing of evidence and admission of evidence which is, of course in the common law tradition, more strict especially if you are working jury trials that that Chamber is more flexible of that and sometimes indicates that although admitted, that while weighing the evidence, it might be of greater or lesser importance. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just two issues very quickly if Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, did you want to respond to this issue we just -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only very briefly. What I wanted to say with regard to the request of the Prosecution was that the time will depend, of course, on the substance of what we shall hear from him. Thank you. No, I was again shorter -- I said that what is requested from the witness -- it does not matter. Yes, exactly. The -- his effort -- hermeneutic report. That from the witness, -- will determine --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, any -- you had two other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President. First, it -- a point of clarification if you would. My understanding is that the Defence will be providing us with two distinct documents, one being a glossary prepared by the expert and a second document being a Defence proposal with respect to how to proceed with respect to the exhibits. If I could, from the Trial Chamber, I would particularly -- or it would be particularly helpful if we could have a date by which those two documents would be available to the Prosecution in one of the official languages of the Tribunal and second, in light of the Chamber's decision announced earlier this morning with respect to time limits, if we could have from the Defence an -- a date on which they expect the expert Radinovic to commence his testimony. It would appear that that would be in light of the Chamber's ruling, Monday of next week, but if we could have that confirmed, and also a deadline for when we would expect these documents from the Defence, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if the -- I invite the parties during the next break that the Defence indicates on what date they would have the -- let's say the exhibits and the glossary ready and if there is still disagreement on the date, the Chamber will give a decision. As far as the appearance of the expert witness is concerned, there of course we cannot finally take a decision but if you would please indicate to the Prosecution when you expect to call the expert witness Radinovic. Yes. Then, is the Defence ready to call its next expert witness? I do understand that that will be Mr. Vilicic; is that correct? Then, Madam usher, could you please escort Dr. Vilicic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Vilicic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are responding in English but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this an indication that you want to testify in English or you would prefer to testify in your native language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd rather give my answers in my native language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... You give your answers in your native language. Before testifying in this Court, Dr. Vilicic, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make the solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text will be handed to you now by madam usher may I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated. Dr. Vilicic, you will first be examined by the counsel for the Defence. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Vilicic.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before I start with my questions, I'd like to ask you to give us your full name and a few words about your professional training?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I'm a mechanical engineer, Janko Vilicic. I have a doctorate in sciences I graduated from mechanical engineering in Belgrade, military mechanical engineering then I completed l'ecole superieure nationale d'armement in France and I also graduated from the engineering mechanical academy in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Vilicic, when you tell us that you defended your doctorate at the technical and military engineering academy in Zagreb, can you tell us what was the subject of your doctoral thesis?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: It was a contribution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask you to make a short break between question and answer. You're speaking the same language and that means that the interpreters will not be able to interpret all you say if you are moving too quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shall repeat. My dissertation had to do with the contribution to the study of combustion in high performance artillery weapons and their effect on the ballistics of those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where did you work?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: As of 1958 I worked at the technical institute head, ballistics sectors, head of the computer sciences sectors and finally I was a deputy chief of R and D for the ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Doctor, in addition to this, were you also a lecturer?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please make a break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I am afraid -- many people forget about this but please try to concentrate. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1961, I was assistant lecturer and lecturer and professor at the faculty of mechanical engineer of the university of Belgrade. I also taught at a mechanical engineering faculty in Sarajevo. I taught at the military academy in Belgrade, post-graduate studies at the engineering military academy in Zagreb. Few two years I lectured in Algiers and a subject I taught was the design of ballistics systems. I was also the mentor for a number of graduate, post-graduate papers, students. I was also a member of a number of commissions, assessing doctoral dissertations in the field of armaments.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you also take part in some practical experiments, if I may ask you that, alongside your theoretical work?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, practically I was, throughout my work, engaged in the research and study and testing of weaponry when I say weaponry, I mean conventional armaments, that is, projectiles, artillery systems. I participated in a number of expert studies of extraordinary events occurring in the -- when weapons are used.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Vilicic, with Dr. Miroljub Vukasinovic and Professor Aleksandar Stamatovic, and you told us that he died 15 days ago, that you did an expert analysis with him, can you tell us, do you still stand by it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I do. We did the expert analysis. We went through all the relevant documentation, all the material that was sent to us, and subsequent information we received from the Defence, witness testimonies and so on, we completed this expert analysis and I handed it over to the Defence in September.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... September 2002 or is it 2001. I ask because the English version of the report is dated 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us when did you complete it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: We finished our analysis in June 2002 and as you know, I participated three times in the examination of expert witnesses. On the basis of -- we studied that material and we concluded there was no need to make any changes in our analysis and we submitted it after we finished with the examination of all those other documents in September 2002. That date is, I suppose, a mistake because ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The title page in English bears the year, it says Belgrade 2002. There is the -- on page 60 we find Belgrade June 26th, 2001. Is that last year on page 60 a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A mistake, yes, quite obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So Professor, will you please tell us what is a mortar?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: A mortar is briefly a weapon with initial angles of 40, 45 degrees so that the drop angles are also larger so the drop angles are over 45, the minimum angles are over 45 degrees and sometimes even over 80 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us, a mortar as a weapon, what parts does it consist of?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: If I may, I brought a number of pictures with me, but they might be time-consuming. If you allow me, perhaps I could put it on the ELMO to show it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, with your leave, the expert wishes to illustrate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have some pictures --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at least we have two pictures of a mortar in the report. If they can be used, fine, but if ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can use them, it's the same photograph, it is a 120 millimetre mortar. Its principal parts are the barrel, the barrel, the base plate, the bipod and the sighting device.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you explain what are the sights, what is a sighting device?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, in our paper, one cannot see it properly so that I will use this photograph, this is an older type of an 82 millimetre mortar and I will show you the sighting device which is an integral part and which is firmly fixed to the bipod of it. As such, it allows to range the fire, to fix the target, and direct the mortar towards the target in case of new sights. When we have old sighting devices, we do not have the optical sights but the so-called collimator which is used to affix the barrel to a point in relation to which later on, when fire is opened, the corrections are made because when a shot has been fired, the barrel jolts until the bipod is stabilised and so that the initial values of the mortar change from one shot to the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your analysis, you quote two types of mortars, that is, 82 millimetres, 120 and a Howitzer type. Can you tell us why did you mention a Howitzer and can one tell apart the effect of a shell fired by a mortar and by a Howitzer?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: There are two reasons why --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No objection to the question and I think we can return to the question but there is one part of the answer to the last question which is not on the transcript and since we might have to move pretty quickly, I would just ask that the witness could repeat it will do it until something is stabilised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it. It's the speed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, when there is a firing that happens, when a mortar is fired, the base plate, until the base plate is stabilised, there is a change of initial elements, initial values, particularly elevation. What happens is that the barrel will change its initial angle, angle of firing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that the base plate does not exactly return in its original position; is that -- after firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The base plate, because it's a nonelastic system, when the firing happens, the pressure of the gunpowder gases will make a pressure on the soil which is why the base plate will be embedded in the soil and this is what we call the stabilisation. Several projectiles having been fired, the base plate will become embedded and stable and will not shift its position. Depending on the ground it will continue to sink up to a point.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So Professor, my question was the reason why you also gave us the example of a Howitzer and is it possible to tell apart the firing from a mortar and firing from a Howitzer, and if that's so, on the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: We gave the Howitzer as an example for two reasons as I've already mentioned. The first reason is that the Howitzer shell is 122 millimetres and in its calibre, it is similar to 120 millimetre shell from a mortar but the main reason -- the main difference is its effect on the target. This projectile, the Howitzer projectile, has a higher drop velocity because of which it goes deeper into the soil when we compare it to a mortar shell, if it is the same kind of soil. The second reason why we mentioned the Howitzer is that we noticed, we observed that the experts of the United Nations -- sorry of UNPROFOR, the UNPROFOR experts, when they assessed one incident of shelling, because of a lack of the firing tables for a mortar, what they used was that they used a Howitzer firing table. I think that that was Verdi. I think that was the name of the lieutenant or captain, Verdi, a French officer who was conducting this analysis of one shelling incident. I have this material, I was given it by the Defence, and we used them. We examined them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I followed you carefully, your answer, but I don't think that I do have your answer, full answer on the differences between the mortar shell and a Howitzer shell. How can you tell the difference between them?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, there are several differences but the main difference is first of all in the mass. The mortar shell of 120 millimetre is about 12.6 to 16 kilograms in terms of its size and mass, while the projectile 122 millimetre is about 21 kilograms mass. The difference is also in the volume of the explosive inside and as I've already said, considering that the Howitzer has a higher initial velocity and also a higher drop velocity when it hits the ground, Howitzer shell compared to the mortar shell goes deeper in the soil and it gives a bigger crater, it produces a larger crater. And it is less efficient, less effective in terms of destruction but -- or rather it is more destructive in terms of terrain but it is less effective in terms of live personnel lethality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Vilicic, could you please repeat the last part of your answer and may I again stress how important it is for the -- both Defence counsel and you, Dr. Vilicic, to make a break. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, what I can see is that the French booth has some difficulty in following the technical nature of this and the speed and I think that we have to be very careful at what is happening so I'm saying this now so that we don't have any problems later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we certainly will, but slowing down will certainly assist all booth to get more time to translate the words of the expert. Could you then please repeat the last part of your answer. I read in the transcript that you said that, "It's less efficient, less effective in terms of destruction but -- or rather it is more destructive in terms of terrain but it's less effective in terms of live personnel," and what did, did you add anything to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said, what I said was that it is more or less the same calibre, 122 is, more or less, the same as the 120 millimetre shell. So it is less effective when compared to a similar calibre shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Vilicic, it might help if you wait until the text on your screen stops moving and then give the answer. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor Vilicic, can you tell us, very briefly, what is the difference between an 82 millimetre mortar and 120 millimetre mortar?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The main difference is the calibre, the calibre; therefore, also in the mass of the projectile. An 82 millimetre shell has got a mass of about 3 kilograms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Vilicic, in your report, you give details of the mass being 3 kilograms and the total mass of a 120 millimetre being 12 kilograms so if you just refer to there's a difference in mass, we all read your report so there's no need to repeat exactly the figures and that speeds up your testimony. But may I, because you are now referring to, I would say, the pages 3 and 5 of your report, I've just one small question in between where you already mentioned the drop velocity. I do not have any explanation for VC but I took that to be the drop velocity and also in the other tables.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, on page 3 of your report you gave the main characteristics of a shell, that is the page 3 of the expert report in B/C/S and my question is: Can you tell us of what parts is a shell made? Professor, you gave us a drawing here, you placed it on the ELMO, can you please clarify, tell us what these parts are?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I will give you a very brief explanation. It has a body, a mortar shell has a body. It has tail stabilisers. It has a fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not really objecting to the professor using a document that he produces from his own store of -- or wealth of documents that he might have but could we be given copies of what he proposes to use in his examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've got two questions. Yes. Okay. Well then you don't have copies at this moment but can you please prepare for the next sequence of the testimony, copies already of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't have copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, not at this moment but I take it you'll prepare them or ask the witness to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, we don't have these documents and we don't have -- we can't have contact with the witness so technically it has to go through the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps then what we could do then is that - I see drawing or documents - at the next break whatever he uses could be copied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Vilicic, could you, during the next break, provide those documents you intend to use to explain your report to the registry so that copies can be made and that we have them available to us as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only problem is that I have many such documents and I don't know whether you will ask me questions about all this but otherwise there's no problem. During the break I can make sure that copies are made if this is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you select those drawings, those documents that you think is most likely that you will use them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So Professor --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes that's what I just wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: This is what a Yugoslav 120 millimetre mortar shell P-61, that is a main high explosive mine for 120 millimetre mortar. As I said, it is made of a body, of the stabiliser, of the fuse, and the main charge in the body of the stabiliser and the additional charges that are inside celluloid shells. There are six additional charges. A mortar shell that are manufactured by Yugoslavia have two types of fuses. The old type UT-M62 its main characteristic is that the coil M75 times 64, that means that the coil is 2 millimetre and there is a newer fuse, UTU-M74 and whose coil is M45 also times two which means that it is the coil of two millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a cry for help from the French booth. They are asking the witness to slow down because it is very technical and the testimony interpretation is getting lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat, I will repeat the main thing for the French booth. It's a filetage. That's the coil, that is the thread of the fuse of the UTU-M62, M25 times 4 times 2 for the fuse UTU-M78 the thread of the coil is M45 times 2. On this drawing, what is given are all the relevant threads of the parts of a mortar shell. Here we can see in the upper part a reductor which has a thread which goes into the body of the -- the body of the shell with a thread M56 times 2, the thread is also 2 millimetres. The mortar projectile has to have a larger opening so that when it is manufactured, the explosive can be cast. The reductor is used in the case when the coil of the fuse is of a smaller radius than the opening of the shell. And in the second case, when the fuse UTU-M74 is a contact fuse, a light contact fuse, then there is no reductor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, since you've explained on this drawing the parts of the shell, can you please tell us how is a shell activated, how does it explode?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The explosion of a shell only occurs after it is fired when, in the course of the firing, the fuse is armed which means that after a certain speeding up, parts of the fuse are moved and they are ready to, upon impact of a shell at a solid obstacle, then the shell becomes detonated and that's when the shell explodes. So in order for a shell to explode, the fuse has to be operational after the shell was fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when you were telling us about the parts of a shell, did I understand you correctly that you were just explaining about the fuse while you did not explain yet all the other parts of the shell?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The only thing I said was what were the main parts of a projectile of a shell. Their function I didn't explain because it is clear that a mortar projectile is stabilised while its trajectory with the help of a stabiliser, which is made of the body of the stabiliser and the tail fins. Inside the stabiliser, we have the main charge, the primary, and additional to that, we have additional charges. In order to fire 120 millimetre shell, we have to use the primary plus one additional charge and then, depending on the distance of a chosen target, we then choose how many additional charges we are going to put on this shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You told us also about how a mortar shell explodes and you told us about a shell becoming activated and the function of the fuse. Can you tell us about the types of fuses that exist in -- that are used for shells? We are talking about 82 millimetre and 122 millimetre shell?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Mortars are used primarily to neutralise troops and firing points. In order to achieve this, two types of fuses are used. There is a contact fuse with immediate operation and also the fuses that are time-delay fuses, except the time-delay fuses have two different functions. We call that or the construction of such a fuse has the so-called tap which is used that before the shell is fired, depending on the target, it is adjusted either to become a contact or a time delay. So that is the coil or the tap on the UTU-M78 fuse. The 82 millimetre mortar shells in most cases are used to destroy troops and that is why they have contact fuses. They can be -- because its greatest efficiency is if a shell explodes on the surface. Mortar projectiles, mortar shells of 120 millimetres are also used to destroy targets that are protected, bunkers, trenches made of wood and soil, they are on time delay and in these cases, that is why we use the fuse which has got a time delay and in that case, the shell will penetrate more deeply into the ground, the depth of penetration will depend on the soil, the resistance of the soil. It has a higher effectiveness in destruction but is less effective in terms of troop destruction so there are fewer fragments that go around the impact site.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, before we have a break, I wanted to ask you a question whether it is possible for a shell not to explode at all and if that is possible, can you tell us in which cases?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible. A shell may not explode only in a case if the fuse is not operational. If there is a so-called misfunctioning of the fuse because of a technical problem, there is a disruption from the initial detonator and the detonator, the fuse so the shell does not explode, the projectile does not explode. The shell remains either embedded or on the surface of the terrain, depending on the terrain, on the soil, it does not explode.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What happens with a shell that doesn't explode?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: In principle, such a shell is very dangerous and it has to be destroyed by placing explosives on it and it then becomes activated and it is destroyed. If the fuse is deactivated which is very risky, then such shell cannot be used again because deformations happen, but what can happen and apparently did happen in war is that the explosive can be taken out, cast out, and it can be used for making other types of shells, the so-called cakes, and then new jackets for shells can be made or other projectiles can be manufactured.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor. I believe it is time for a break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will adjourn until 11.00, and may I invite you, Dr. Vilicic, to provide the documents most likely to be used to the registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam usher, will you please escort Dr. Vilicic into the courtroom. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, before the break, you explained to us what happens to a shell that doesn't explode and I think that you explained that it can be used or reused and how it can be reused again. Now, my question is what is the effect of a shell on the target?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: As I have already explained, a mortar projectile is used to destroy troops and also to destroy sheltered facilities and mostly firing points, machine-gun nests and so on. A mortar projectile has -- primarily it's the fragments that are effective.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Professor, what does the efficiency of a shell depend on?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The effectiveness on the shell on the target will depend on the characteristics of a shell in its construction so it will depend on the quality of the material of the jacket.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you've already explained that in detail in your report. What I wanted to hear from you is just the most general points so that we can follow you.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The effectiveness of a shell, of a mortar shell will depend on the features, the characteristics of the projectile, and also of the features,, characteristics, that is, the resistance of the target itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, on the picture 2.7 you gave us the main parameters of the probability of target destruction. Can you tell us how many fragments are obtained from a shell explosion? You've already put that in table number 5 but I just wanted to have answer to this question?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll be very brief because it was in -- on page 9 in the report, it's given how many an 82 millimetre calibre shell, that is, 120 millimetre calibre shell, what their mass of the explosive is in these, it's already given and also what is the mass of the fragments and that is the 7 --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: For 82 millimetre, is it 289 fragments?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The mass of fragments is -- the total mass of fragments is 2.000, that is the mass of the metal jacket, 2.290. But during the explosion, one part of the mass is lost and the mass of fragments which is actually effective on the target is. As it is given 2.019, that is on a mortar shell of 120, that will be from the mass of the shell, the mass of the fragments will be 8.338. In table 4, I just have to say that -- I have to make an observation, what has been given is the velocity of the fragment, the initial velocity of the fragments at the time of the explosion while on table 5, what -- the value that is important is the coefficient of the charge that is the relation or the ratio between steel and explosive. What I said earlier was that a mortar shell of 120 millimetre calibre is more effective, relatively more effective than 122 artillery projectile. This conclusion is drawn on the basis of the fact that a mortar shell has a larger coefficient of charge. Because of this, the metal jacket of the projectile is fragmented into a higher number of fragments compared to an artillery projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, in your report, on page 17 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Sorry, I have a question because if not, afterwards it's more difficult. That table, table number 5, you have the mass of lost fragments for mortar shells 82, 120 and 122 millimetres. In the first case is 11,8 and the second is 0,8, I think that that's wrong. It should be 20.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. That's correct. It's a mistake. This should be 20. And in the third column it should be 23 for an artillery shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, first of all, on page 9 of the English version, you said the energy of the fragments of 100 joules, can you please tell us what is the energy, what does it represent?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The energy of 100 joules by centimetres square is adopted, established energy which we know is lethal, is effective, it is lethal energy. It's internationally adopted, it's something that's been established in military technology as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, on page 17 of your report, 17, 18, and 19, you mention the terms resistance of the target --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, if you would just allow me. Dr. Vilicic, you just corrected your table number 5 saying that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- That mass of lost fragments should be 20 for a 120 millimetre shell and that it should be 23 for an artillery shell. Would you explain to me why it would not be 2.3 but 23? So I am talking about the second correction you made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as you can see, the total mass of material -- metal parts 10.265 and then after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... After the second correction you made you were asked about the 0.2 and then you added in the column for the artillery shell, 122 millimetre, 2.3 should be 23. I'm asking you why it should be 23 rather than 2.3? So would you please concentrate on the last correction you made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me, the total, the total mass of metal parts, 122 millimetre shells, that is the very last column, it's 18.075.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The recovery is 17.659. The difference is 4.043. When we divide that by 18.075 is 0.22, that is 0.223, 0.22 times 100 is 22 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid you are mixing up the number and the mass, the 4.043 is the number of recovered fragments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. Yes, I apologise, I was looking at...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I see is the total mass of metal parts is 18.075 grams whereas the total mass of recovered fragments is 17.659 which is in my view correctly you state that the mass of lost fragments is 2.3 per cent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, 2.3 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your second correction, we forget about that? It's not 23, it's just 2.3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2.3, yes, that's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you explain to us the term of a target resistance and the sensitivity of the fuse, and these two terms, how do you link them, can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: For a fuse to be operational and to function, what is necessary is that the target has a certain resistance. If the target has a high level of resistance or high degree of resistance then when the impact occurs, the fuse upon an impact, when it is high resistance of the target then it will be -- what will happen is that the -- a fuse will be activated very quickly, that is, the fuse will become armed and the explosion will occur. If the target is less resistant for instance, a soil or a swamp, agricultural land, then the time that we need for the fuse to become armed and to function, the time will be longer and to penetrate -- it will penetrate more deeply into the terrain and then the explosion will occur later. That is the less resistant terrains will make it so that more -- less resistant terrains will make it so that the fuse will be activated later and the explosion will occur slightly later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, isn't this perfectly explained in paragraph 2, 4 and especially on page 19 by the difference in resistance of the targets?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I'm aware of that but I just wanted to explain certain basic given data of this report so we can follow Mr. Vilicic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, what can you tell us, why fragmentation happens, why the -- why this happens?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Fragmentation happens for many reasons. First of all because of the changes of the characteristics of the gunpowder fuse and this will depend on the year of the manufacture, of the year of the charge being filled and the outside temperature, then also what will happen is that the mass of the projectile can change from -- deviate from that of the table and also because of the age of the system which is used to fire, the artillery system, the state of repair, and in the end, of course, the weather conditions during the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, can you tell us, what is the method that you used to calculate the value of the fragments, of the fragmentation?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: In all of these cases of our analysis, of our report, according to the documents that we received regarding mortars, mortar shells, to see the fragmentation, that is the deviation from the trajectory, we used the table, the firing tables for 82 and 120 millimetre mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Ms. Pilipovic, your question was translated into English: "Can you tell us what is the method that you used to calculate the value of the fragments, of the fragmentation." It's not clear to me what you mean by the value of the fragments or the value of the fragmentation. Are you talking about the number of fragments or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, here, we are speaking about the fragmentation of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So what is the method that you calculated to establish the value of the projectile fragmentation, that was my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean by "What calculation did you have in mind?" Because we have on the fragmentation the dispersion of fragments we have the mass of fragments we have a lot of calculation and -- but what is exactly the value of fragments?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The dispersion of fragments on the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Vilicic, you seem to understand the question, how did you understand to what calculations was referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the transcript, it's been mistranslated. The question was translated as fragmentation of projectile. What it is, it's dispersion of fragments, it is dispersion of fragments of -- of fragments of the projectile on the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I now understand the question. It's a translation problem. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us what is the main characteristics of the 82 and 120 millimetre mortar shells of Yugoslav manufacture?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: 82 and 120 millimetre calibre mortar shells of Yugoslav manufacture are not very different from other mortars, 82 and 120 millimetre mortars of foreign manufacture but the main characteristic of our mortar shells that we analysed and used to analyse for all of -- in all of these cases is the fact that the mortar projectiles of Yugoslav manufacture had coils with a 2 millimetre thread for the reductor, for the fuse, for the body of the stabiliser which is screwed into the body of the shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when you mentioned the stabiliser, can you tell us what is the velocity of the ejection of the stabiliser, that is, at which speed is the stabiliser ejected?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: During the explosion of a mortar shell, the explosive charge has a frontal effect on the stabiliser and the impact wave is trying to stop the stabiliser, to eject it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I ask -- may I return to your earlier question and especially to the answer and I have some difficulties in interpreting the answer, that is, Dr. Vilicic, you said that, "mortar projectiles of Yugoslav manufacture had coils with a 2 millimetre thread for the reductor, for the fuse, for the body of the stabiliser which is screwed into the body of the shell." Were you referring to the reductor for screwing in the fuse or is that the same thread as used by screwing in the tail fin because you are talking about two parts of the shell and you are talking about the reductor. Is the reductor used both for the tail fin and for the fuse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The reductor is used only at the top of the shell, for the fuse. It is intended to stop the opening of the mine and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. And then you in that same answer also referred to the stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you intend to say that for screwing in the stabiliser, the same thread was used but not with the reductor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. No, there is no need to use a reductor. It is screwed in directly into the body of the mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was unclear to me and now it's clear to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Into the body of the shell, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'm not sure you've answered my previous question regarding the velocity with which the stabiliser is rejected or jettisoned?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to answer your question. It is a relative velocity with which during an explosion, the stabiliser is able to return to the opposite -- into the opposite direction, opposite as opposed to the firing direction depending, of course, on the velocity, impact velocity of the projectile. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what that velocity would be after the explosion, the stabiliser rejection velocity and why would it be important to establish that velocity at all?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: In our analysis, we provided a detailed explanation as to how the stabiliser is jettisoned. I'm just going to repeat here the order of magnitude of these velocities. The velocity with which the stabiliser is rejected is anywhere - of course depending on the quality of the charge and the weight of the stabiliser - between 140 and 170 metres per second. As far as our 120 millimetre shell is concerned, we used, in our analysis, the velocity, the rejection velocity of 154 metres per second which velocity was obtained on the basis of the calculation which is exposed in our report. It is possible for the stabiliser to remain in place if the impact velocity of the shell is between 140 and 170 metres per second, but it can also be jettisoned if the impact velocity of the shell is lower than this value.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, I would like you to tell the Chamber and explain to all of us what traces are left on soil after the explosion of the shell, what are they called and what do they depend on?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: In our terminology, the place of impact of a shell is called a crater. During the explosion of a mortar projectile, metal parts of the jacket are dispersed and in accordance with very detailed examination that we conducted when we obtained these projectiles, under an angle of the equatorial line of 57 degrees, it is on that angle that metal parts of a jacket are dispersed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'm not sure you have answered my question as to the parameters of the depth of the crater, what does it depend on?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: It depends on the resistance of the soil, the impact velocity and the time necessary for the fuse to be activated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is the significance of establishing the depth of a crater?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The depth of a crater is very significant for the purposes of establishing the following. First of all, the type of projectile that was used, that is, it will depend -- on the basis of the width and depth of the crater, one can establish the type of the projectile which was used and in the five cases that we analysed, mortar projectiles were examined, therefore, the craters of an 82 calibre projectile were smaller, of course, than the crater caused by the 120 millimetre calibre provided that both projectiles fell on the same type of soil.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Professor, you told us that the depth of a crater left by an 82 calibre projectile is smaller than the one left by a 120 millimetre calibre. Can you tell us what these two depths are, that is, the depths of the crater left by these two projectiles?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, the depth of the crater depends on the impact velocity of the projectile and the resistance of the soil. In order to establish the exact depth of a crater one needs to know what type of a projectile was used, the angle under which the projectile hit the soil, and the drop velocity of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, this is all explained clearly in table 7, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but I wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... That the Chamber has really read the reports with full attention and therefore if you ask a question about --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I trust you have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... What the crater depth would be then of course the expert could do nothing else than referring to the variables that are establishing the crater depth as set out IN table 7 and he has now to repeat that it depends on the drop angle, on the drop velocity, on the type of soil on which it lands and that's all in table 7, so that really is clear to the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, after the explosion of the shell, is it possible for the stabiliser to become embedded in the soil?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I have already indicated, under certain circumstances, it is possible for the stabiliser to become embedded in the soil. This would happen whenever the drop velocity of a projectile is higher than the velocity with which the stabiliser was rejected, that is, higher than the velocity that I indicated, the one that is higher than 140 to 170 metres per second.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I believe you have already clarified the velocity with which the stabiliser is embedded in the soil depends on but I would be grateful if you could repeat that for us?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I believe I already said that. It depends on the drop velocity and the soil resistance and of course on the velocity of the stabiliser, which continues to move in that case in the direction of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, as far as these two calibres are concerned, 82 and 120, what would be the penetrating velocity of the stabiliser on tarmac, on asphalt soil?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: In our analysis in table -- we indicated the penetration velocity of a projectile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, may I just ask you to -- it's not quite clear to me what you understand by penetrating velocity. Velocity, is as far as I understand, speed, a projectile or a tail fin with a certain speed could penetrate or not and penetrate to a smaller or to a higher degree into a certain soil. Before the expert answers the question, could you, Ms. Pilipovic, explain to us quite clearly what you understand by the term penetration velocity, velocity, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't ask about the penetration velocity but the depth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have a -- then we have a problem of translation and that might happen sometimes in this very technical matter because most of our interpreters are not educated in a technical university, neither was I, so let's try to get things clear. You are asking about depth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The depth of penetration of an 82 calibre and 120 calibre projectile stabiliser on a macadam asphalt cover.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, doesn't the report of this expert already clearly explain that the penetration depth would certainly depend on the drop velocity and the back power so could this be a question that could be answered in general terms or should we specify?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, as regards the question concerning a macadam asphalt cover, that type of soil. I'm trying to be as clear as possible and I believe that my question was specific enough.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: In the analysis in table 7 and table 8, we provided the depth of penetration. As far as the stabiliser penetration depth in macadam soil or macadam asphalt covered soil, I must emphasise the possibility of some very old asphalt to be more resistant than a concrete surface; therefore, the depth of penetration, as I have already indicated, will depend on the drop velocity of the stabiliser, on the velocity of the stabiliser itself, and the angle under which it penetrates. By way of illustration, I can perhaps tell you that in case of 120 calibre projectile stabiliser, when the impact angle is 55.6, which is the maximum impact angle for this type of charge, 600, depending once again on the drop velocity, the highest value would be up to 10 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Once again it appears to me that the Professor is referring to documents that he has perhaps they could be put on the ELMO so I could see what he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you are consulting any documents, Dr. Vilicic, and I can imagine that you didn't learn all figures by heart, but the parties and the Chamber would like to know what type of document you are consulting and before doing so, would you just allow me to reread your last answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction page 43, line 23, not 600, but the sixth charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you just give me 30 seconds to read and to try to better understand the last answer. May I ask you one question in respect of your last answer. You said that the maximum drop angle would be 55.6, that is what I also find in your table number 2 for 0 plus 6 charges the drop angle 55.6. Would that be valid also if the level of firing in the terrain would be different from the level of impact, for example, you can fire from sea level and the impact could be 300 metres above sea level or you could fire from 500 metres above sea level and the impact could be at 200 metres above sea level. Would your values in table 2 be valid also for these situation and I'm especially referring to the figures under 2.6, A, B and C which seem to describe trajectory where the level of firing is the same as the level of impact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the difference, as far as the drop velocity's concerned, when the firing position of the weapon is above the height of the target in cases of between 250 metres is very small. The results will have to take into account the gravity for that height.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that, apart from influence the drop velocity, also influence the angle, the drop angle slightly or significantly but...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It changes only slightly the angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Your Honours will allow me, I would like to show you the graph of the trajectory of 120 millimetre shell when the angle is not zero but is below the level of the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the sketch that you placed on the ELMO, can you explain what you wanted to explain?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President asked me about the difference in the angle of descent for the -- depending on the altitude of the weapons up to 500 metres. This is a zero altitude. If the target is at 500 metres below, then we can see from here that these are the trajectories for the top group of the angles, the highest angle of descent and we can see that the differences in the angle of descent are very slight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see. So you say it has slight impact of the angle of descent and it has some impact on the basis of the gravity on the speed of impact. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I think that in answering the question that I asked you, you used the table which you've just put on the ELMO. Can you please finish answering that question? This is the table which is currently on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the numerical part of that table is given in here. If you mean the firing table, do you mean the -- or the depth of penetration.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The depth of penetration, that is the question that we didn't get an answer to, I believe, the full answer.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Please do, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: You asked about the depth of penetration for a stabiliser in the soil which is a macadam covered by layer of asphalt, and my answer was that the asphalt is relatively soft as a principle, however old asphalt can be very hard and it can actually behave as it was a concrete surface. In the table that we can see on the ELMO, the depth of penetration is given for macadam soil, macadam surface, how much it can be depending on the drop velocity. This is the column that I'm just pointing to now, where you can see that for the depth of penetration or 20 centimetres, the velocity of the stabiliser should be 127 metres. And here, we are speaking about the sixth charge which is the maximum angle of descent for the sixth charge. The maximum impact velocity, drop velocity, impact velocity is 235 metres. If we take that off from the stabiliser 140, then we will only have left 90 metres per second which is the speed of the velocity of the stabiliser. From this table you can see that practically the stabiliser cannot penetrate 20 centimetres, it cannot even penetrate 15 centimetres into such a surface. It penetrates to a much lesser degree. If there was a layer of old asphalt, then the depth of penetration would be even less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
