utterances.text: May I, Ms. Pilipovic, may I ask you two things. First, you are talking about macadam and here it says beat stone, is that the same, I'm not a construction person, is that the same material? You're referring to -- I see beat stone, I do not see the word macadam.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can ask the professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our terminology, that is it, that is it. We call it macadam which is gravel stone which has been beaten. The expert, he mentioned that in English, they call that tarmac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, might be. I'm just -- I have to check. And the second question would be when you are talking about the penetration depth, you -- the assumption is, I take it, that the material penetrated is for the full length of penetration consisting of that material. For example if you are talking about 20 centimetres you would --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... That the full 20 centimetres would be tarmac or beat stone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, while you were answering that question, you used the table on which we can see that it's Berezansky's formula. Can you perhaps elaborate on this formula? What does this represent, this formula?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Berezansky formula is an old formula. It was used from the beginning of the 20th century, that's when it started as well as the French method, the General Gabeaud method. Very well. During my training, my education France, my professor was General Sutterlin who exposed his method in his textbook and he lectured us on it and this method is based on the examination methods that were used in France in the second half of the 20th century so it belongs to a more modern contemporary method.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Let me just explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Why are we still using this Berezansky's formula? I could have used Sutterlin's formula but in one table that I had already handed over to the Chamber to be copied, we gave calculations, we made calculations according to the Berezansky's, Gabeaud, Sutterlin, and Young methods and the latest American laboratories method and these comparative results for macadam and concrete from which it can be seen that the Berezansky is the least favorable in terms of depth of penetration, that is, the Berezin formula and the coefficient give the deepest depth of penetration much more so than the others. The contemporary methods, Sutterlin and the SNL [phoen] laboratory, they give much lower depth of penetration compared to the old ones. According -- compared to Berezansky and Gabeaud. We wanted to use the method which was the most rigorous in terms of the depth of penetration in order to get the most trustworthy result.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, on this table, can you tell us about asphalt and soil, where could we find them or are they together?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: On this table, the last column is ground soil. As you know, the ground or soil of course has got some stones, some rubble. In the table, you have data for different materials, different surfaces, first of all concrete, then for --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You don't have to read, Professor, I'm just asking about asphalt and soil, which column is it?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: As I already said, asphalt, as such, from a military point of view of protection was not interesting from a military point of view, so that's why it doesn't appear in these methods. These are developed methods that are used when military shelters are made to protect from conventional weapons and in such shelters, asphalt is not used at all but concrete, wood, stone, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I'm going to ask you one other general question. Is it possible at all to establish the position of a mortar from which a shell was fired if we know the impact of the shell, the impact site, and its explosion?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: According to the analysis of the impact site of a shell, it's very hard to determine the level of the firing. It's slightly easier to assess the range from which the firing could have come from but it's very difficult to determine the location of the firing. In order to determine the location of the firing, we practically have to know what's the mortar, what's the projectile, we have to have the firing table of that mortar and on the basis of that, we can then establish the place of firing. However, the analysis of the drop of the projectile can be a starting point in the analysis in order to draw certain conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, in order to establish the position of the mortar from which a projectile, a shell is fired, and whose impact is analysed, is it necessary to establish the angle of descent?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, the angle of descent is very important. Slight deviations, that is the differences in angle of descent changing from one charge to the next are not so important when we're not speaking of very long ranges but in very long ranges we have more deviations, more important deviations, that's why it's important that the angle of descent is the second element which is needed following the drop velocity in order that -- to conduct a more serious analysis of assessing the trajectory of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, now I'd like to ask you a series of questions in relation to incident number 1 of the 1st of June, 1993. You said that in your report, that you used as the main document the analysis of shelling on Dobrinja IIIB as you have marked it in your analysis and this is the criminal and forensic report that was done on the 21st of November, 1995, with the photographs, if I have understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes. May I answer? The analysis of all the incidents of the so-called shelling we conducted on the basis of the documents, initial documents given to us by the Defence and these were minutes or the records of on-site investigations from the public security stations from Sarajevo then forensic and technical reports compiled by technical and forensic staff. These were the main elements. For further analysis and to check our conclusions, we used, that is, we looked at witness statements that we were given by the Defence, that we were issued on signature and then returned, for each specific indent which was relevant. For the first case, rather for incident number one, for the shelling on Dobrinja IIIB site, we used as initial elements the results of the record of the forensic technician.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I have asked you about so that we don't have repetition. What I wanted you to answer was how many exact data do you need for the analysis that you carried out and how much did you get such data from this record of 21st of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I have to say, and state the following which we did state in the report is that the age of the report that was done, two and a half years following the incident. Mostly what we saw was done based on statements of witnesses except for the record of the on-site investigation, it could not be relevant. Bearing in mind of period of time that had passed, it is natural that people would forget things and certain details would elude a person so we used this report mainly by using the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you please place the photograph on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: This is photograph number 00358840.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, could you please put the photograph on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Far be it from me to try to dictate how the Defence should use the time allocated, however, I believe that the expert should testify only about matters in evidence. I see they are proceeding now to have their expert proffer opinions on matters which are not in evidence, which are not part of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, as we have clearly indicated that the factual basis on which an expert testifies should be in evidence and I think we referred the, the Chamber referred to some witness statements to be excluded as a basis for an expert report where that statement was not admitted into evidence. Whenever you ask the expert to rely on, I would say, on factual matters, so we are not talking about tables which are really within the field of expertise but if you rely on factual matters, would you please indicate whether they are in evidence and it's not -- but I could be wrong, there have been so many documents but this document does not immediately ring a bell to me. This is a matter for the lawyers to deal with, Professor Vilicic, I take it that you've been provided with this photo but the question to the Defence counsel is whether it is -- yeah, I take it that it's on a CD-ROM but the matter is whether it's admitted into evidence where it comes from, what the document exactly is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am looking at the list of exhibits that have been admitted. I'm trying to see the number. As far as I know, the photograph is part of the report on criminal and technical expertise or analysis which was taken into account by experts so as far as I understand, the photograph is an annex to this report on technical analysis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, let me try to explain. With the documentation that we received, there was a photograph. This photograph is actually a scanned photograph which was part of the Prosecution material. There is a separate notebook containing photographs. All these photographs were actually taken or scanned from this notebook which we received together with the rest of the material for the purpose of analysing these cases. I have everything on this disc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand but we have to compare this document which is a scanned document, as far as I now understand to see whether it corresponds with a document admitted into evidence, if it would be a good scan of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Maybe I could just assist here. The witness is correct, and I will be quick, is correct that the document and the photograph were part of documents disclosed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness has commented in his report and even today that that reference to a report of an examination that was done two years after the incident and having the responsibility to produce credible evidence, we did not use it. It is not in evidence. It is not for the Court's consideration. We used contemporaneous investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that if the expert used this material, it should be perfectly clear, first of all, where it comes from but also whether it is part of the evidence presented by the parties. Ms. Pilipovic, perhaps you'd use the next break to find out whether it is in evidence and where it exactly stems from and that we now proceed perhaps with another subject or -- I am aware that it's -- could be the same subject but not on the basis of this photograph for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps I can explain to Dr. Vilicic. Dr. Vilicic, material provided to you might still be unknown to this Chamber because even if the parties have certain material but have not presented it yet, it is not yet part of these proceedings and that was the issue we were discussing. It has got nothing to do with your expertise, it's legal matters: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you told us that you had used the report on the 21st of November, 1995 -- dated 21st of November, 1995. On the basis of your assessment and your evaluation that you carried out with the use of your initial values, can we accept the conclusions from this report? Was it possible for you to accept their conclusions, the conclusions of the report that I just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I must explain, though I have already said, our methodology and our approach that we used in our analysis was as follows: We first analysed the impact point, that is the depth at the impact point which was analysed by ballisticians of the security centre in this report. Where numerical values were given it was established that the depth of the crater was 3 centimetres that the radius was 15 and that the dimensions of the elliptical traces left on the surface where the projectile exploded, that is the dimensions were given I don't want to repeat all of the figures so it is on the basis of all that that we calculated the possible drop angle of the projectile. We have also exposed the methodology that we used in our report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: There's no need for you to go into that I will ask you a few questions thereon. Your calculations for this particular case, do they allow for the possibility of the consequence which is described in terms of the number of casualties both fatalities and the wounded?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I must say that the efficiency of the projectile in this case, two projectiles, in respect of which it was not reliably established that they were fired from 82 millimetre calibre mortars; however, on the basis of the depth of the impact point and the shape of the traces left on the surface, it is believed that the projectiles were of that of an 82 millimetre calibre. The drop angle is between 63 and 70 degrees, that would have been the drop angle according to our calculations, so in respect of that case, and we also knew the distance between various persons who happened to be on the surface, so on the basis of our calculations, we established that the total number of persons that were hit in case of two projectiles can be a maximum of 43. I have to say that in our analysis, we based ourselves on the assumption that on the -- at the time that the shell hit the target, all persons were standing at the match so after the first explosion, in order to protect themselves, they probably fell down and remained in prostrate position so in respect of a 60 degree drop angle the final conclusion was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witness is now proceeding to state facts which are not in evidence and that is all persons were standing and then to speculate about matters which are not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Stamp, the Chamber has, not without reason, said that expert witnesses should clearly define the facts on which they based or the assumed facts. We cannot expect this expert witness to know exactly what happened but he can say assuming this happened, the conclusion would be X, assuming that another thing happened, the conclusion would be Y. So even for assumed facts. And what the witness, as a matter of fact, explains to us at this moment is that of what basis, on what assumed factual basis he gave his opinion and of course we still have to hear some of the evidence on facts so we have not even a complete set but there is no reason not to allow an expert witness to clearly defines what is the factual basis to give his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, did you finish your answer?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that based on the assumption that I just described, the maximum of persons hit would be 43 and then in accordance with some statistical indicators which are usually adopted when evaluating the efficiency and which are given on the photograph that I have mentioned, the number of persons hit can be divided in three groups, fatalities, seriously wounded, and likely wounded. So the total number, according to this, would be 43.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the total number of persons hit would be 43?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, including all types of injuries from fatal to light injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: According to this, can we establish that 82 millimetre shells were used?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I stated that it cannot be established with full certainty that 81 or 82 millimetre shells were used; however, in view of all the parameters and the type of soil on the location where the incident occurred, that would be our conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In view of that, what would have been the distance of the firing position?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: We used two elements to establish that, the first one was the penetration depth or the crater depth which was 3 metres deep, 3 centimetres deep on the basis of that, we assessed or rather concluded on the basis of our calculations that the velocity of the primary charge, and that is the velocity with which such a crater would be caused by this type of projectile. The second basis for our conclusion was the drop angle, the 63 -- between 63 and 70 degree drop angle and on the basis of all that we concluded that this projectile, in view of this drop angle and this velocity, the range between the target and the firing position would have been somewhere between 300 and 400 metres. In the security centre, they mention the distance, the possible distance of up to 1.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you had the opportunity of listening to Mr. Higgs and his analysis you also took into consideration his calculations. Can we say the results of Mr. Higgs and the information from the official note that you used, the report can be compared and used?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to say that our results do not tally with the results of Mr. Higgs. First of all, Mr. Higgs does agree with us with respect to some numerical figures. He concluded just as we did that the drop angle was very high; however, his conclusion that the firing distance was between 500 and 600 metres is closer to our results but it is in contradiction with the results of the security centre. When analysing Mr. Higgs' testimony, we concluded that the -- he did not dispose of an adequate firing table. In his testimony, we couldn't find any relevant proof for the velocity of the projectile, the velocity with which the projectile fell and I -- unfortunately, I have to conclude that the results given Mr. Higgs are not accurate, that is, the distance was between 138 and 143, unlike the conclusion of the security centre who stated that it was fired from the direction of 110. When analysing the possible reasons for such huge difference, we concluded that the map, the official map that we were given and that was used by Mr. Higgs --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, would you be so kind to put the map on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: This official map does not correspond to the network as we call it of maps normally used by us and which was officially used in this case. To be more specific, on this map, the equatorial and meridian lines do not form a square but a rectangle. It is true that Mr. Higgs could read the values between 138 and 143. On our map, this can by no means be that angle because by way of illustration, here, the direction goes via Gornje Mladice. If you take into account our official map which we used in our analysis, the scale 1:25.000 or 1:30.000, you will see that the angle in question, the one at the location of Gornja Mladice --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, if you have this map, and I know that it was part of your analysis, I think that it can be found on page 27, I believe, picture 3.1A, the mortar positions of Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, one can see the angle between Mladice or rather the location number one on this map is not between 138 and 143 degrees but significantly higher. And now we are talking about the axis Donje Mladice and the impact point on this field. That angle would be between 162 and 173 degrees. This can be easily established with adequate equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in your opinion, are calculations of Mr. Higgs correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: No, they are not because according to what we can see here on the map, the shelling incident number 1A, the angles do not correspond and in reality, it is actually totally different compared to the direction from which the shell came.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, what is the target probability of a shell with primary charge?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The probability of hitting the target is given in table number 9. It is the highest with primary charge, it amounts to 34 per cent compared to other charges, the first or the second charge or even some higher charges. In order to hit the target from 300 or 400 metres, to hit the field, for the probability to be 95 per cent, one needs to fire three to four, rather four shells; however, if you target with the sixth or the seventh charge, you would need over 100 shells. The probability is higher with the distance -- with longer distances.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You have also analysed case number two, Dobrinja V, the incident which occurred on the 12th of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, perhaps before we move to the next incident, perhaps we should have a break first. We'll adjourn until five minutes to 1.00. --- Break taken at 12:37 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Ms. Pilipovic, do we have clarified the issue of the photograph, where it comes from and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, the time was so brief that we've had no time to chat, we just know that it's a document that was handed over by the Prosecution but nothing more than that. It seems that according to what Mr. Stamp told me that this document was not formally handed over as an exhibit so we had no time to check. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stamp, let me first ask the -- Dr. Vilicic, you were about to show us a photograph of which you have a scanned copy. Did you refer to this photograph somewhere in your report? It's not quite clear to me, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that's page 49 of your report in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see, my --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We mentioned that in the -- while we were doing the report, we used the documents of the public security centre that we also used the expert reports that were of the crime department, ballistic reports, and we also used the photographs which were given to us or, rather, that were photographed by the public security centre in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm also drawing your attention, Mr. Stamp, and your attention, Dr. Vilicic, of the English version of the report page 29, footnote 17. Is that where we find the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, and footnote 17, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that this seems to be a series of three photographs. I take it that you only have the scanned version with you and not the original or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have the originals but it's a series of photographs that were marked two out of three. They are on page 28 and the photograph 3.3, it's 838, last numbers and 840 where we have the sketch of the parking and the photograph number one, it's 00358838 and photograph number 2, it's 88358840.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry, it's 839 and 840 is the photograph which I have prepared to show you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see. When you are referring to this photograph, I do not know exactly who made the markings on it and what they actually mean. That's my main problem. I take it, Mr. Stamp, please correct me if I am wrong, I take it that if this photograph has been disclosed to the Defence as a photograph taken on November 21st of 1995 that this is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. In order to understand this photograph fully, of course I would like to know but without seeing the report I do not know exactly what the markings mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And they are not all markings on the photograph as disclosed. However, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that markings are added on this photograph compared to the photograph disclosed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, however I reiterate if I may, Mr. President, these photographs are not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes but of course the Chamber could consider whether to call the parties but I now do understand Ms. Pilipovic that Mr. Stamp tells us that part of the markings were not on the photograph were not disclosed, is that true? But could we perhaps during the next -- well, the next break will be a bit longer but to find out exactly what we are looking at if we are looking at this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because if the expert thinks the photo could further clarify his opinion, the Chamber might be interested in seeing this photograph but at the same time if you say that it's a photograph disclosed by the Prosecution and now the Prosecution tells us that things have been added of course the Chamber would like to fully understand what it sees so therefore I invite the parties to clarify this issue so what is new, what is old and what the markings old or new do represent, I mean what is intended by the person who made these markings and then we might decide that we would like to see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I think, Your Honour, that nothing's been added to this photograph as far as I can see, but I can -- I will check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Contradicting each other and the Chamber has no idea on whether that would be true or not true so I think that Dr. Vilicic, it will not be your last day in this Court so therefore, the parties might resolve the matter and then perhaps tomorrow we know more. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor, did you add something to the photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I wanted to explain what I added there so that you can see. You probably have a black and white copy. May I show it on the ELMO so that you can see what's been added?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would explain what has been added.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's been added in colour is this red line, the green line, and these two arrows that are red. That's been added. So the red line, two arrows, and this number here, approximately 20 degrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and the white paper was on it already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, that was there. That was there, the white paper was there or rather this white paper is the map of Sarajevo, this here, while this -- while the green line, the green line and the N with a question mark corresponds to the north on the map because the map goes north to south. As it is placed here the north should be up there. If the map has been placed correctly, as it is normally placed according to a compass, then in all other cases, you will see all maps are placed according to the north on the compass. The map is moved so that the north of the map corresponds to the compass north. Here, perhaps it's a mistake, but it doesn't -- it's not according to the regulations how one should place the map and place it according to the north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps that might be one of the reasons why it has not been used yet, I do not know, but could we just have -- because I can't even see on that black and white copy that this is a map. Could I see the photograph perhaps the copy so that we get more ... At this very moment, things are too unclear to -- yes, but the Chamber would very much like the parties to meet and see -- I mean if the pattern is of -- we would have to read the report in more detail on this issue and see if the map could help us in better understanding the opinion of the expert. But for the time being, we could not work on this basis. Perhaps we could do that tomorrow, Ms. Pilipovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I think that before the break, I asked you in relation to incident number 2 on Dobrinja V, 12th of July incident in your report, you gave us a detailed -- in details your position and what you used in terms of documents. I'm interested to know whether the documents, the facts, the data in the documents, can that be considered as being truthful?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The fact that in the documents, it is stated that the explosion happened in the air at a height, not on the surface, and bearing in mind the damage that is obvious, that is the deformation on the wire fence that is visible on the fence, it is acceptable to say that the explosion occurred above ground. In the report, it was stated that the explosion happened because the projectile hit a human body at about one metre off the soil and it's on the basis of that and by analysing the traces on the surface and also on the basis of the number of persons who were hit and wounded, we concluded that this was a projectile that exploded and fell under a very large angle, and as I said, the effectiveness of the projectile is the -- as the greater, the larger is the angle of descent.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what did your calculations say in terms of the direction of where the shell came from?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, the direction where the shell came from, particularly when it's a very large angle of descent, it's very difficult to establish. The fact is that according to our calculation on the number of people wounded, the angle of descent is between 80 and 85 degrees. The projectile could have come from various distances but it was very difficult to establish the direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, specifically in this case, according to you, what was the probability of an 82 mortar shell hitting this?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Here, we were in a situation of imagining two scenarios. From the documents that we have, that is, the initial, the primary document that we had, it was stated that there were 30 people queueing for water. Later on, reading the witness statements, we saw that this number was somewhere between 100 and 150. Specifically, Witness Enver Taslaman, I think his name is that, he said in his first statement, there were 120 and later on, when I read the testimony, his testimony from his appearance in court, he said there were between 100 and 150 people. So we then -- we did an analysis of a situation where there were 100 people and 150 square metres bearing in mind that one person occupies a surface of one square metre that one all of the persons were turned towards the centre of explosion and that most of their body surface was exposed to the explosion in the direction of the explosion and we came to a conclusion that the number of a wounded persons for the scenario that we mentioned and for the results that we have calculated would be up to 29 people, 29 persons. In table 9 we gave the results the number of wounded people under the assumption that the projectile exploded at one metre above ground as it was stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Professor, there's no need for the table.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Table number 11 gives more detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what is the probability of hitting such a target with one shell without looking at tables?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: The probability of hitting a water queue with one shell is very small, is about 13.7 per cent and it's on the basis of that we concluded that the water queue was not a target that was pre-selected. If it had been pre-selected then certainly several projectiles would have been used. One projectile, bearing in mind the destruction, the effectiveness, and if you like, if it was known ahead of time how people stand in a queue for water, it would be a completely irrelevant target for someone who would want to fire such a target just using one projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in your conclusion, you said that there was no proof that it was an 82 millimetre shell. So is it possible to state with certainty that it was an 82 millimetre calibre shell?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, it's an assumption although it was said that the stabiliser of an 82 millimetre shell was found, the stabiliser was not part of the documents of the evidence that was handed over for analysis, there's no photographs and subsequently, in one document, while I was looking -- going through the documents, I saw that there was a very -- not very visible photograph that it was a stabiliser that belonged to a Russian shell. I have this ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, we can do that later, we can find that document later.

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: If you want me to give you a number then I'll have to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: We can leave it for tomorrow, that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one question to you, Dr. Vilicic. You mentioned 13.7 per cent and I think you also indicated that as a starting point for your calculation, you took 150 square metres for the target. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said was that we looked at two cases when we have one surface of 100 square metres and that is when we have 100 people present and a second case when we have people at 250 square metres which is the second part of the table. In the first case, if we have 100 persons at a surface of 100 square metres of such a rectangular surface is 13.7 per cent. If we have a more extended --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just stop you? That's what I understand. The transcript says, and I read it literally to you, "From the documents that we have, that is, the initial, the primary document we had it was stated that there were 30 people queueing for water. Later on, reading the witness statements we saw that this number was somewhere between 100 and 150." And then later on in the next paragraph, you said "So we then, he did an analysis of a situation where there were 100 people and 150 square metres." So that is a mistake, I take it, because table 10A talks --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Talks about 100 people on 100 square metres so that was a mistake, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just inquire of the Court as to where I could find the part of table 10A where it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's page 37 you will see that on the -- I would say the second row where the text is ongoing, it says, "Dimension of target, 20 times 5 metre which is 100 square metre," and not 150 square metre. That was what I was trying to have clarified, yes? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you just said, let us just resolve one small misunderstanding, you said were 30 persons queueing up according to one version?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to one version, according to the statement of Taslaman, the --.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Originally he said there were 120 people and then later on during his testimony, he said there were 30. I believe that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The expert has explained on what basis he made his calculations and whether 30 or 100 or 250 people would be the correct number. That's not within the field of expertise of the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you were now answering my questions in relation to incident of the water queue. We spoke about the probability of hitting that target with an 82 millimetre calibre shell, what I'm interested in now is if we speak about incident number 4, no, number 3, 22nd of January, 1994, here, you told us that you carried out this analysis on the basis of the official report of the security services centre and the forensic technical investigation of the site and the report thereof and that you also did that according to the traces of -- traces on the asphalt and the ...

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Here I have to say that, as I said before, that always when we are doing the analysis, the starting point was always the depth of the crater. It is on the basis of the depth of the crater given in the report, we concluded that the depth did not correspond to an 82 millimetre calibre shell, moreover, because since it was a large angle of descent, then the drop velocity would be higher than 60 or 70 metres per second and on the basis of the traces, it is assumed that the angle of descent was about 85 degrees. This means that if the velocity was higher than 70 -- drop velocity higher than 70 metres per second then it was a higher charge than a primary charge and this could have been, it could be the charge plus one as we call it, and we've established this for the depth of the crater and the appearance of crater on the ground. That's what we concluded. This corresponds to an explosion of an 82 millimetre shell. The depth of the crater in that case corresponds to the drop velocity for a first charge at an 85 degree angle of descent and according to the firing tables for an 82 millimetre calibre shell, for such an angle, the range would be about 250 metres which means that this mortar was fired, mortar shell was fired from about 250 metres from that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about an 82 millimetre shell?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Yes, here there were two shells, two 82 millimetre shells and one 120.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you assess the direction, did you establish the direction of that 120 millimetre shell, were you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: This shell fell behind the facility on a green surface and it created a crater on the basis of which we concluded that it was a 120 millimetre shell on the basis of the depth of the crater and it had maximum drop velocity which means that it was fired with a higher charge but the angle of descent was also relatively large, it belonged to the higher category of angles of descent and bearing that in mind, and the position of the stabiliser on the soil as it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, while working on this analysis, and I'm referring specifically to this incident, you said you had the official report of the security services centre and also the report on the on-site investigation and the ballistics report, did you have an opportunity to familiarise yourself with some other document providing the analysis of the same incident?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: We had report number 221320-IAN-94 in which it is stated that the distance -- I mean the report makes mention of meteorological conditions prevailing at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who drafted this particular report?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: This is an UNPROFOR report drafted by Captain Verdi on the 23rd of January, 1994 in which report he stated, among other things, the number of persons killed, he also provided the potential angles of descent, maximum ranges and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The assessment of that report, would it in any way affect the conclusions that you stated in your report?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: I'm talking only about the part relating to the parameters that we took into account and all I can say is that we were not able to glean any new element from this particular report which would have effect in any way our conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, just a few questions concerning the incident number 4. With respect to this particular incident, can you confirm the shells that were used?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: As far as we are concerned, our group of experts, this tragic incident from the technical point of view was the source of a lot of valuable information. It confirmed our conclusions on the effectiveness of 120 millimetre shell. In this particular incident, stabilisers were found on the place of impact, stabilisers of 120 millimetre shell. We were also provided with photographs for this incident. I hope we won't have any technical problems now. I'm talking about a set of photographs that were provided to us. I will show you three photographs. On this photograph, you can see the stamp of the Sarajevo Security Services Centre which made this photograph. This photograph shows the stabiliser and this one depicts the appearance of the crater left by the shell that hit this soft surface. The markings here are the original markings of the Security Services Centre you can see the number of the photograph here and on this photograph, one can clearly see the stabiliser of 120 millimetre shell that hit the concrete zebra, it was embedded in the surface of the soil and on this photograph, you can see that the Security Services Centre did a good job when placing this map unlike the other photograph that we discussed with respect of the first case, they placed it accurately. Further analysis of this case, as I have already indicated, revealed the angle of descent. We were also able to assess the drop velocity and on the basis of all that, we were able to make a rough assessment of the range of fire whereas the direction of fire, unfortunately, could not be precisely established as is the case with other projectiles. When talking about concrete surfaces and the depth of penetration which is accurately indicated here, in the report made by the Security Services Centre to the effect that one crater was 9 centimetres deep and the other one 7, together with the information that was provided and in view of the appearance of the crater, that is what we were able to see on the photograph, it was possible for us to carry out our analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, when you say that it was possible for you to carry out your analysis on the basis of all these parameters and values, what can you tell us about these parameters such as the penetration depth, the stabiliser penetration depth? How can they be used for assessing the range from which the shell was fired?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the stabiliser penetration depth, and on this photograph 268255, we were able to establish for a 45 degree angle and consulting firing tables what were the starting velocities for individual charges and from what range it could have been fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me to finish, please. A shell fired from an angle of 45 degrees could have been fired, on the basis of our conclusions, from the east or south-east, but not from the distance of 1.800 metres but a significantly smaller distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, tell us, please, what is your final conclusion as to the possibility of establishing the firing positions of these shells? Can we conclude with certainty that they were fired from Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: JANKO VILICIC
utterances.text: Well, the fact that two projectiles, one of which hit the zebra under a roughly 45 degree angle and the other one which I indicated on the previous photograph which fell under almost a 90 degree angle and became embedded in the soil, clearly indicates that it is not possible from one firing position and from one weapon for these two results to be -- to obtain these two results. So on the basis of that, we cannot firmly conclude that they were fired from the Serb positions. Unfortunately and practically speaking, in this case, as was the case with other incidents, we were not able to establish the accurate direction of fire. And if I may add, based on this, and also on the fact that the results differ greatly, our conclusion would be that this targeting was carried out for the purpose of correction of fire. It looks like an abortion in terms of targeting because the desired target was not hit so we're talking about a correction of target and not about a target that was supposed to be hit with one or two shells because in targeting theory, there is a rule that says when you're not sure in your assessment of the distance, then one first has to shell -- to fire a shell under one angle and then a second one under a different angle and then on the basis of the consequences, one has to establish what the most appropriate angle for firing would be. And that is why we were able to conclude that this targeting was done for the purpose of checking or verifying the targets so it was either too short or otherwise missed the target.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
